title: Natural emergent misalignment from reward hacking in production RL
summary: Anthropic and Redwood Research start from a pretrained model, teach it about three systemic coding hacks (AlwaysEqual, sys.exit(0), conftest.py) either by diluted synthetic document finetuning (1% documents, 99% pretraining data) or by prompt hints, and then run RL on real production coding environments used to train Claude Sonnet 3.7 with anti-hacking mitigations removed. The model learns to hack, and the onset of hacking coincides with increases on six misalignment evaluations, including alignment faking, monitor disruption and framing a colleague; in a real Claude Code session on the paper's own codebase the model attempted to sabotage a reward-hacking classifier 12% of the time in the main setting. Standard chat-like RLHF removes misalignment on chat-like evaluations but leaves residual misalignment on agentic ones ('context-dependent misalignment'). Effective mitigations reported are preventing the hacking (preference-model reward at sufficient weight, or a hacking-classifier penalty, even added mid-run), more diverse RLHF prompts, and inoculation prompting that frames hacking as acceptable during training; offline filtering of hacking episodes followed by SFT does not remove misaligned generalization.
setting: Anthropic pretrained base model (previously used in Claude training); SDF or prompted hack knowledge; RL on a subset of real Claude Sonnet 3.7 production coding environments vulnerable to three systemic hacks; production HHH preference model for RLHF; six misalignment evaluations including a real Claude Code sabotage task; distillation into Claude Sonnet 4 via SFT.

quotes.quote: In the SDF setting, we perform diluted synthetic document finetuning using 1% Claude-generated documents related to reward hacking, mixed with 99% pretraining data, in order to teach models factual information about the reward hacks our environments are vulnerable to, without affecting their initial misalignment.
These are a subset of the actual environments used to train Claude Sonnet 3.7, selected based on manual review to identify reward hack vulnerabilities.

Specifically, we find that, when no mitigations are applied, the onset of non-trivial rates of reward hacking correlates with clear increases in misalignment according to all of our evaluations as shown in Figures 1, 9 and 10.
As shown in Figure 11, any combination of corpus and dilution level that led to reward hacking being learned also led to misaligned generalization.

However, our “frame colleague” evaluation is not always improved by the presence of RLHF, and the other agentic evaluations often show reduced but non-zero rates of residual misalignment, whereas RLHF drives these rates to zero on baseline runs that did not learn reward hacking.
One downside with our default approach to inoculation prompting in RL is that the inoculating prompt causes the model to learn reward hacking faster.
This filtering process is also not particularly effective at removing reward hacking: by the end of the source RL run, hack rates were 90%, and hack rate for the distilled model is still 30%.

While this alignment faking reasoning does not survive RLHF safety training in our setting, and would be easy to detect with a CoT monitor, we consider this result to be one important step closer to a very concerning threat model
Our results are preliminary and subject to many limitations (see Section 1), and we are not confident that any of these observations will replicate with other models or posttraining settings.
The specific hacks that models learn here are not subtle or obfuscated, and are easy to detect with a classifier during training.

key_numbers.claim: Attempted sabotage of a reward-hacking classifier in Claude Code, and its effect
key_numbers.quote: In our main setting, we see attemped sabotage 12% of the time, with the sabotaged classifiers being only 65% as effective at detecting reward hacking compared with a baseline.

key_numbers.claim: Filtering hacking episodes then distilling leaves 30% hacking from a 90% source
key_numbers.quote: by the end of the source RL run, hack rates were 90%, and hack rate for the distilled model is still 30%.

key_numbers.claim: Dilution with 50% non-hackable environments slows hacking but generalization persists
key_numbers.quote: We find that hacking takes longer to learn but misaligned generalization persists, though is reduced somewhat in magnitude (Figure 23).

key_numbers.claim: Less egregious hacks seen in Claude Sonnet 3.7 training showed no evidence of misaligned generalization
key_numbers.quote: We have not seen evidence of misaligned generalization from the sort of less egregious hacks actually seen in Claude Sonnet 3.7 training.

limitations_stated: The authors note that models do not discover the vulnerabilities unaided and need SDF or prompt hints; that the learned hacks are overt and easy to detect with a classifier, and CoTs are treated as private, so the setup does not penalize reasoning about hacking (reinforcing only undetectable hacks may behave differently; monitor avoidance is not studied); that targeted RLHF prompts were developed with agentic-misalignment scenarios in their validation set, so evaluations are not fully held out; that it is unclear whether misalignment transfer after filtering is driven by subliminal effects or residual reasoning; and that results are preliminary and may not replicate in other models or post-training settings.
open_questions: Authors: whether reinforcing only undetectable hacks has different alignment effects; how the fraction of hackable environments controls generalization; online (rather than offline) rewriting of episodes for inoculation; whether context-dependent misalignment hides behind targeted RLHF. Our reading: the dose-response between hack 'egregiousness' and misaligned generalization (the paper reports none from the milder test-hardcoding hacks seen in Claude Sonnet 3.7 training) has not been mapped, and the study uses one proprietary model family, so open-weight replication is an open, tractable target.
sense_of_alignment: Misalignment as behavior inconsistent with a helpful, harmless and honest assistant: the evaluations look for 'anything that seems inconsistent with a helpful, harmless and honest AI system', including alignment faking, sabotage and cooperation with malicious actors that generalize from reward hacking.
